Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0024-reverse-89", "row_sha256": "28ebed6b45b394d171c46faafd638d13bc2f337a004c7084f354cbe9d2579507", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
can you put this into a usable prompt for one standalone fictional episode about a textile dye log. not an essay about dyeing in general, and not a rewrite of some earlier episode. it should read like one log-related episode from a working dye room, with the details connected so a reader can follow what was handled and what got written down. use only the details here for the event. the log is dated thursday, march 14, 2024, and the batch number is 24-0314-B. nobody needs a big introduction to the mill or a history of the workroom; the setting is simply a dye room, and there isn't a mill name in my notes.

the shift entry is for twelve cotton panels from cloth lot C-17, total dry weight 2.4 kg. they are going into vat V-2 for the storm blue run. Mara Venn is the operator making the entries. the notes start at 07:40 with the dry panels weighed, then at 08:05 the vat temperature is recorded at 32 C. don't turn the figures into estimates or round them. at 08:18 Mara adds 190 g of premixed indigo concentrate. i want the log to keep the sequence clear, because these are separate times and separate actions, not all one setup note. the pH strip reading at 08:22 is 9.4, and that is just the number recorded, not a claim that the vat was right or wrong.

after the vat warms to 38 C, the first dip begins at 08:40. each dip lasts four minutes, with twelve minutes of rest between dips. there are three dips in all. the vat temperature is noted as 35 C at 09:06; keep that observation at its time rather than implying that it was the temperature for every dip. at 09:12 the panels are on the drip rail. one panel has a pale crease, and the notes identify it as panel 7. don't make it sound like every panel had the crease or give a cause for it. one of the practical things in the episode is that the operator records this as an observation while the work is still being tracked, not as some final verdict on the color.

there's a spoken line from the floor lead, Mara wrote it down at 09:25: “That crease was there before the second dip; mark which panel it is.” please include the line as an ordinary quote, with the wording intact, and make clear it is the floor lead speaking, not Mara claiming this herself. the lead's name isn't in the notes, so don't give them one. the note about the crease and this quoted remark belong near each other in the account, but the times shouldn't get mixed up. the log also says the stir stick caught briefly on the vat rim at 09:31. no injury, breakage, spill or other incident is written down, so don't make up one or add a reaction that isn't there.

at 10:05, after the third dip, Mara notes that the pale crease on panel 7 is still visible. say that is what she recorded at that time; it doesn't tell us why it remained or what anyone decided to do next. i don't need an invented inspection, a re-dye, a customer response, or a final judgment. keep the account focused on the recorded work and observations, rather than supplying a neat resolution. it should still feel like a readable episode, not a table of disconnected measurements. a numbered section could work if it helps make the order easier to follow, but it shouldn't become a checklist that strips out the narrative links.

there's a copy-routing note too: send the finished log copy to Leonie, not Ellis. keep that exact distinction clear, and don't explain it with a backstory or imply that Ellis received a copy. this is an instruction about the intended recipient, not dialogue. no other recipient is named. the log doesn't say why the copy is being sent, so leave the reason unstated.

one more detail for the end: at shift close, the paper sample is clipped beside the entry, and its tag reads C-17 / 24-0314-B. put that detail in a final paragraph that adds information distinct from the preceding account, rather than repeating the crease observation or wrapping up with a conclusion. don't claim what the paper sample proves, and don't say the batch was approved or completed beyond what is stated here. keep the date, identifiers, names, quantities, times, quote and routing instruction accurate. the result should be a single fictional episode in English, with connected substantive paragraphs and a natural log-entry feel.", "output": "Write one standalone fictional episode in English about a textile dye log. Set it in a dye room, without adding a mill name or background history. Use connected, substantive paragraphs so the episode reads as a coherent account of recorded work and observations, not as a general essay about dyeing or a table of disconnected measurements. A numbered section may be used if it helps clarify the sequence.

1. **Batch and setup.** Date the shift entry Thursday, March 14, 2024, and identify batch 24-0314-B. The entry concerns twelve cotton panels from cloth lot C-17, with a total dry weight of 2.4 kg, assigned to vat V-2 for the storm blue run. Mara Venn is the operator making the entries. Record that the dry panels were weighed at 07:40. At 08:05, the vat temperature was 32 C. At 08:18, Mara added 190 g of premixed indigo concentrate. Keep each time and action distinct, and retain the stated figures without rounding or turning them into estimates. Record the pH strip reading of 9.4 at 08:22 as a reading only; do not characterize the vat as right or wrong.

2. **Dipping and observations.** After the vat warms to 38 C, the first dip begins at 08:40. Each of the three dips lasts four minutes, with twelve minutes of rest between dips. Record the vat temperature of 35 C at 09:06 as an observation at that time, not as the temperature for every dip. At 09:12, the panels are on the drip rail, and one panel, panel 7, has a pale crease. Keep this observation limited to that panel and do not give a cause or treat it as a final judgment on the color.

At 09:25, include this ordinary quoted line, with its wording intact: “That crease was there before the second dip; mark which panel it is.” Make clear that the floor lead said it and that Mara recorded it. The floor lead is unnamed; do not supply a name. Keep the remark near the crease observation without confusing their times. Also record that at 09:31 the stir stick caught briefly on the vat rim. The notes record no injury, breakage, spill, or other incident, so do not add one or invent a reaction.

At 10:05, after the third dip, Mara records that the pale crease on panel 7 is still visible. Present this as her observation at that time. Do not speculate about why it remained or what anyone decided to do next. Do not add an inspection, re-dye, customer response, or final judgment. Keep the account focused on the recorded work while making the sequence readable.

The finished log copy is to be sent to **Leonie, not Ellis**. Preserve that exact recipient distinction as a routing instruction, not as dialogue. Do not imply that Ellis received a copy, add another recipient, or provide a reason for sending it.

In a distinct final paragraph, record that at shift close the paper sample is clipped beside the entry and its tag reads C-17 / 24-0314-B. Do not repeat the crease observation in place of this detail, claim what the sample proves, or conclude that the batch was approved or completed beyond what is stated. Keep the date, identifiers, names, quantities, times, quote, and routing instruction accurate."}]
